EED is an obligate, non-catalytic subunit of PRC2: its WD40 domain binds H3K27me3 and allosterically stimulates the EZH2 methyltransferase, which sustains the repressive mark. Losing EED therefore collapses PRC2 activity and erases H3K27me3 across Polycomb-repressed loci — the order matters: EED loss first, H3K27me3 depletion second, and only then transcriptional de-repression. Scin is a CDX2 target that carries Polycomb repression in this context, so once the H3K27me3 lock is removed the locus becomes accessible and permissive, letting the existing/available CDX2 pool bind and activate it rather than any new CDX2 activity being required. Net effect: derepression plus CDX2-driven activation both push Scin in the same direction, so expression goes up relative to the matched unperturbed control.

down

TP63 is a positive regulator of NABP2: p63 family proteins (TAp63/ΔNp63α) occupy p63 response elements in target promoters/enhancers and recruit co-activators such as p300/CBP plus the basal transcriptional machinery, so NABP2 transcription depends on continued p63 occupancy. Order of events after the perturbation: TP63 loss → the activator is no longer bound at the NABP2 regulatory region and co-activator recruitment/active chromatin marks are lost → reduced RNA Pol II initiation and elongation at the NABP2 locus → falling NABP2 mRNA and, consequently, lower hSSB1 protein (which is also short-lived and further destabilized when the DNA-damage-response context that normally supports it is lost). The key mediator is therefore the p63-dependent transactivation input itself, not an indirect signaling relay, so the matched control comparison shows NABP2 going down rather than up.

down

ESR1 (estrogen receptor α) acts as a ligand-activated transcription factor that binds estrogen response elements at the CISH regulatory site and recruits coactivators to drive CISH transcription. Removing or reducing that regulatory site abolishes ESR1 occupancy, so the activating input to the CISH promoter/enhancer is lost and the gene is transcribed at a lower rate. The order is: site loss → loss of ESR1 binding and coactivator recruitment → reduced transcriptional initiation → lower steady-state CISH mRNA. In the matched unperturbed control the site is intact, so ESR1 maintains the higher baseline expression; hence CISH goes down relative to that control.

down

GATA1 R216Q is a hypomorphic missense change in the N‑terminal zinc finger that weakens GATA1's ability to engage palindromic GATA elements and to recruit cofactors such as FOG1. Because the transcription factor acts upstream as an activator of Lrrc39 — the variant protein binds the gene's regulatory region less effectively and/or assembles a less productive activation complex — the rate of Lrrc39 transcription falls, and its steady-state mRNA is therefore lower than in the matched unperturbed control. The order is: variant GATA1 → impaired DNA binding/cofactor recruitment → reduced transactivation at the Lrrc39 locus → decreased Lrrc39 expression.

up

TWIST1 drives expression of the miR-10b hairpin from the Hox cluster, and mature miR-10b loads into an Argonaute-containing RISC that base-pairs with the HOXD10 3′UTR, recruiting deadenylation and translational repression of that transcript. So the ordering in the intact circuit is TWIST1 → miR-10b → reduced HOXD10 protein and mRNA. Removing or knocking down miR-10b severs the middle link: the HOXD10 transcript is no longer targeted for RISC-mediated silencing, so it accumulates and HOXD10 expression rises relative to the matched control — a classic loss-of-microRNA de-repression, with the effect being post-transcriptional and therefore visible even when the HOXD10 locus itself is not transcriptionally re-activated.

down

ESR1 acts as an activating transcription factor at the P2RY2 locus, binding a cis-regulatory enhancer element (P2RY2e) and recruiting coactivators (e.g., steroid receptor coactivators, p300/CBP) that maintain an open, H3K27ac-marked chromatin state and load RNA polymerase II at the P2RY2 promoter. When that element is lost or reduced, the ESR1-dependent activating input is removed, so the enhancer–promoter looping that sustains constitutive P2RY2 transcription weakens. The causal order is: enhancer loss/reduction → loss of ESR1 binding and coactivator recruitment → reduced chromatin accessibility and Pol II pause release at the promoter → decreased P2RY2 mRNA output relative to the matched unperturbed control. Note the direction assumes the mechanism is activating (the usual case for an estrogen-receptor-bound enhancer driving its target); if ESR1 were instead repressive at this element, the loss-of-element result would flip, so the enhancer's direction of effect — not merely its occupancy — is the key determinant.

Up.

PPARα (NR1C1) is a ligand-activated nuclear receptor, and Hmgcs2 — the rate-limiting enzyme of ketogenesis — is a canonical PPARα target. Under gain-or-activation conditions the order is: ligand (fasting-derived free fatty acids, or a synthetic agonist such as WY-14643/fenofibrate) binds the PPARα ligand-binding domain → PPARα heterodimerizes with RXR and binds the PPRE (DR1 element) in the Hmgcs2 promoter/enhancer → coactivators (PGC-1α, SRC-1) are recruited and chromatin is remodeled → Hmgcs2 transcription increases, raising Hmgcs2 mRNA and protein, which in turn drives hepatic ketone-body production. Because PPARα acts directly on the Hmgcs2 promoter rather than through a repressive intermediate, the net effect on Hmgcs2 expression relative to the matched unperturbed control is positive.

down

ZNF143 is a sequence-specific DNA-binding transcription factor that acts primarily as a transcriptional activator: it binds TTC/CT-rich motifs in proximal promoters and stimulates RNA polymerase II initiation, so its canonical direct targets lose expression when it is depleted. Loss or reduction of ZNF143 (CRISPR/RNAi knockdown, auxin-inducible degron degradation, or a dominant-negative) therefore removes the activating input at the ADAT3 promoter. Mechanistically the order is: ZNF143 protein level falls → its activating module is no longer recruited to the ADAT3 promoter/regulatory element → transcription initiation and promoter-proximal Pol II pausing/elongation are reduced (cofactor-dependent; ZNF143 works with general initiation machinery and SAGA-type coactivators rather than through a repressive intermediate) → mature ADAT3 mRNA steady-state level declines relative to the matched unperturbed control. The one caveat worth flagging is that ZNF143 can act as a cis-repressor at a small subset of its sites, where it occludes initiation elements and competes with stronger activators; if ADAT3 were bound in that "repressed" configuration rather than at a canonical activating promoter, depletion would instead raise ADAT3. Given ADAT3 is a ubiquitously expressed tRNA-modifying enzyme with a housekeeping-type promoter, the activating configuration is the expected context, so the predicted direction is down.

down

ZNF143 is a sequence-specific transcriptional activator (a C2H2 zinc-finger protein that binds the "SPH" motif with its co-factor SBF/SPT20 in the STAF complex). It acts in the nucleus, at DNA, upstream of the transcript — it recruits the STAF assembly and general transcription machinery to promoters and also anchors chromatin loops that bring enhancers to their target promoters. BIRC5 (survivin) is one of its direct targets: the ZNF143 site sits in the BIRC5 promoter/regulatory region, so ZNF143 occupancy is what supplies the activating input to that gene. Remove ZNF143 and the promoter loses its activator, the loop/enhancer contact weakens, transcription initiation falls, and the mature BIRC5 mRNA follows the primary transcript down. The causal order is therefore: loss of ZNF143 protein → loss of promoter/loop occupancy → reduced transcription initiation at BIRC5 → lower BIRC5 mRNA and survivin protein. Because ZNF143 provides positive, not repressive, input, the direction is down rather than up; note only that an indirect secondary route (e.g., loss of a ZNF143-dependent repressor) could partially blunt the drop, but it would not reverse it.

down

ZNF143 (zinc-finger protein 143) acts as a sequence-specific transcriptional activator: it occupies the promoter of CNIH1 through its cognate SBS motif and, once bound, recruits coactivators and general transcription machinery to drive polymerase II initiation. CNIH1 therefore sits downstream of ZNF143 as a positively regulated target, so the causal order runs ZNF143 occupancy → promoter activation → CNIH1 transcription. When ZNF143 is lost or reduced, promoter occupancy at the CNIH1 locus falls, coactivator recruitment and Pol II loading at that promoter drop, and the steady-state CNIH1 mRNA decreases — hence the expected direction is down rather than up.

down

ZNF143 acts as a transcriptional activator, not a repressor: it binds its cognate SBS motif (a CCAAT-box-like element) in the promoter of CYB5R1 and, together with general/promoter-associated coactivators at chromatin-loop anchors, sustains RNA polymerase II occupancy and productive initiation. When ZNF143 is lost or reduced, the promoter loses that activating input, so the order of events runs: ZNF143 depletion → loss of promoter binding/occupancy at the CYB5R1 locus → reduced Pol II recruitment and initiation → decreased CYB5R1 mRNA (and consequently lower cytochrome b5 reductase 1 protein). Because the mechanism is loss of a positive regulator rather than relief of repression, the matched unperturbed control should show higher CYB5R1 expression than the perturbed sample; i.e., CYB5R1 goes down.

down.

ZNF143 (also called SBF/STAF) is a CCAAT-box-binding **transcriptional activator**: it occupies promoters/enhancers of its targets, recruits coactivators and RNA Pol II, and supports promoter–enhancer looping through cohesin. FASTK is a direct ZNF143 target, so its baseline transcription depends on ZNF143 being present and DNA-bound. The causal order is: loss/reduction of ZNF143 → loss of ZNF143 occupancy at the FASTK regulatory region and disassembly of the activation complex (activator loss, not repression gain) → decreased Pol II loading / transcription initiation at the FASTK locus → lower steady-state FASTK mRNA and protein. Because the perturbation removes a positive regulator rather than inducing a repressor, the expected direction relative to the matched unperturbed control is a decrease in FASTK expression.

down

ZNF143 is a sequence-specific activator that binds SBS (SphI-site) motifs in the promoters and enhancers of its target genes, where it promotes RNA polymerase II recruitment and transcription initiation. Loss or reduction of ZNF143 therefore removes a positive input at the HSPA14 locus, the causal chain running: ZNF143 depletion → reduced ZNF143 occupancy at the HSPA14 regulatory region → weakened promoter/enhancer activation and lower Pol II loading → decreased HSPA14 transcription → lower HSPA14 mRNA (and subsequently protein) relative to the matched unperturbed control. Because ZNF143 acts upstream as an activating trans-factor rather than as a downstream effector, the effect on HSPA14 is a direct consequence of the perturbation, not a secondary or compensatory response; any indirect stress-responsive buffering (HSPA14 being an HSP70-family chaperone) would, if anything, only partially offset the primary drop, not reverse it. (Caveat: this assumes the activating mode reported for ZNF143 at this locus; a repressive/insulator context would invert the sign.)

down

ZNF143 acts as a transcriptional activator, binding SBS (SphI-binding-site) motifs in promoters and enhancers and recruiting coactivators that promote RNA polymerase II initiation and elongation. Loss or reduction of ZNF143 therefore removes the positive regulator from the KLC2 regulatory element: the causal order is (1) reduced ZNF143 occupancy at the KLC2 promoter/enhancer, (2) loss of coactivator recruitment and diminished chromatin accessibility, (3) decreased Pol II loading and transcription, (4) lower steady-state KLC2 mRNA. Relative to the matched unperturbed control in the same context, KLC2 expression is expected to go down.

down

ZNF143 (zinc finger protein 143) acts as a sequence-specific transcriptional activator, binding its cognate motif in the promoter/regulatory region of target genes and recruiting coactivators to drive RNA polymerase II initiation. In the unperturbed state, ZNF143 occupancy at the MRPL54 locus sustains its basal transcription, so MRPL54 mRNA is produced at a ZNF143-dependent level. When ZNF143 is lost or reduced, the activating input at that site is removed: enhancer/promoter occupancy drops, coactivator recruitment falls, and the rate of MRPL54 transcription decreases. The causal order is therefore ZNF143 depletion → loss of promoter-bound activation complex → reduced Pol II initiation at MRPL54 → lower steady-state MRPL54 mRNA (with the corresponding protein and mitochondrial ribosome subunit following later). The key mediators are ZNF143 itself as the DNA-binding activator and the general transcriptional machinery it recruits; no indirect repressive intermediate is required, because the direction simply mirrors the sign of the regulatory edge — a positive regulator removed means its target goes down.

down

ZNF143 is a sequence-specific activator that binds the SPH/SBS motif in promoters and enhancers and promotes promoter–enhancer looping and RNA polymerase II recruitment, so PNKD is a positively regulated target. Reducing ZNF143 (CRISPR knockout, knockdown, or degradation) removes that activation: occupancy at the PNKD regulatory element falls first, promoter–enhancer contact and Pol II loading at the PNKD promoter decrease next, and mature PNKD transcript and protein levels follow downward. Because the mechanism is loss of a required activator rather than loss of a repressor, the expected direction is a decrease relative to the matched unperturbed control.

down

ZNF143 (also called SBF/Staf) is a sequence-specific C2H2 zinc-finger protein that binds the SPH motif (GTGCNNNGTG) at target promoters and functions as a transcriptional activator, recruiting coactivators and general transcription factors and helping establish promoter–enhancer looping. Because the ZNF143→PTPMT1 link is an activating one, reducing ZNF143 abundance lowers its occupancy at the PTPMT1 promoter, so coactivator recruitment and transcription initiation fall and PTPMT1 mRNA (and subsequently protein) drops relative to the matched unperturbed control. Order of events: ZNF143 loss → reduced promoter occupancy/loop formation → decreased transcriptional activation → lower PTPMT1 output. (This holds if ZNF143 is the direct activating regulator; were it repressive at this locus, the direction would invert, but its canonical role at PTPMT1-type promoters is activation.)

down

ZNF143 is a sequence-specific activator that binds CCAAT-like and related motifs in promoters of ribosomal protein genes, so RPL6 transcription depends on ZNF143 occupancy for normal output. Reducing ZNF143 lowers its binding at the RPL6 promoter, which decreases recruitment of coactivators and RNA polymerase II and therefore reduces RPL6 mRNA synthesis; with no compensating feedback, steady-state RPL6 expression falls below the matched unperturbed control. Order: ZNF143 loss → reduced promoter occupancy → less Pol II/coactivator recruitment → decreased transcription → lower RPL6 levels.

down

ZNF143 is a promoter-associated activator — it binds CCAAT-like SBS motifs at promoters of snRNA, tRNA and protein-coding genes and recruits the general transcriptional machinery (and coactivators such as SNAPC/Pol III and Pol II components). SGF29 is a subunit of the SAGA histone acetyltransferase module (the HAT module also containing GCN5 and ADA2), so ZNF143 binding at the SGF29 promoter supports its transcription. On loss or reduction of ZNF143, the activating complex is no longer recruited to that promoter, so SGF29 transcription initiation drops and mature SGF29 mRNA falls relative to the matched unperturbed control. Order of events: ZNF143 depletion → loss of promoter occupancy and coactivator recruitment → reduced SGF29 transcription → decreased steady-state SGF29 expression. (This assumes the annotated interaction is activating, as ZNF143's characterized role implies; the mechanism field was blank, so a repressive relationship cannot be excluded from the metadata alone.)

down

ZNF143 (hStaf) is a C2H2 zinc-finger transcription factor that binds the Staf-binding site (SBS) in the promoters of a large fraction of human genes and works as a promoter-bound activator. Mechanistically, ZNF143 binds its motif at the promoter, recruits cofactors (e.g., the HCFC1/THAP11 complex) and facilitates RNA polymerase II initiation — rapid degron-mediated depletion of ZNF143 causes loss of Pol II initiation and reduced output at its activated targets, while only a smaller subset of genes is de-repressed. Because SSB is catalogued here as a ZNF143 target, the parsimonious interpretation with no other mechanism specified is that ZNF143 acts as an upstream activator of SSB transcription; in the causal order ZNF143 loss → reduced promoter occupancy/initiation at the SSB promoter → less SSB mRNA and protein. The caveat is that ZNF143 can also repress a minority of targets in cis, so if SSB were in that repressed class the direction would invert — but the default, activation-based expectation is a decrease.

down

ZNF143 (also called SBF/STAF) binds the promoter-proximal SBS/STAF motif and acts as a transcriptional activator, so the causal chain is: ZNF143 protein loss → loss of ZNF143 occupancy at the TMEM258 regulatory element → reduced recruitment of coactivators (e.g., p300/CBP, Mediator) and reduced RNA Pol II initiation/release at the TMEM258 promoter → decreased TMEM258 mRNA. Without a described mechanism field this is the default expectation for an activating TF; the direction would only flip (up) if ZNF143 were instead documented as a repressor at this locus, which is not the standard annotation. Order: perturbation → loss of TF binding → loss of activation → lower steady-state TMEM258 expression, relative to the matched unperturbed control.

down

ZNF143 acts as a transcriptional activator, so removing it lowers UQCR10 rather than raising it. Mechanistically, the order is: ZNF143 protein is depleted → its binding site in the UQCR10 promoter/regulatory region (ZNF143 recognizes the SPH/SBS-type motif, GTGCNNCTCC-like, which it shares with CTCF at many promoters) loses occupancy → loss of the activating signal ZNF143 normally provides, including recruitment/stabilization of RNA polymerase II and its role in promoter–enhancer looping → reduced initiation of UQCR10 transcription → less UQCR10 mRNA, and consequently less UQCR10 protein (a complex III subunit). Because ZNF143 functions as the positive mediator here and no compensatory activator was described, the matched unperturbed control should sit higher than the ZNF143-depleted sample, i.e. UQCR10 goes down after the loss-of-function perturbation. Note this reasoning assumes ZNF143 is a net activator at this locus; if the annotated regulatory link were instead repressive, the direction would invert.

down

ZNF143 (also called SBF/STAF) is a C2H2 zinc-finger transcription factor that binds a specific DNA consensus in promoters and acts as a transcriptional activator, typically stabilized at its sites through interactions with the cohesin/CTCF machinery that promotes enhancer–promoter looping. Because the annotated regulatory relationship here is ZNF143 → ZNF24, ZNF143 occupies the ZNF24 regulatory region and drives its transcription. In a loss-or-reduction perturbation the causal order is: reduced ZNF143 protein → loss of activator occupancy at the ZNF24 promoter/regulatory element → decreased recruitment of coactivators and looping-dependent transcription → lower ZNF24 mRNA. The key mediator is therefore the ZNF143 activator complex itself (not a repressor being relieved), so the matched unperturbed control is expected to sit higher than the perturbed sample, and ZNF24 expression is expected to go down.

down

ZNF143 is a sequence-specific zinc-finger transcription factor that normally occupies the ZNF746 promoter and supplies an activating input, so removing it strips the locus of a positive regulator rather than releasing it from repression. The causal order is: loss of ZNF143 protein → reduced ZNF143 occupancy at the ZNF746 promoter → diminished coactivator and RNA polymerase II recruitment → lower ZNF746 transcription → lower steady-state ZNF746 mRNA relative to the matched unperturbed control. Because this link is activating, the target tracks the regulator's direction, i.e., it falls.

up

Mechanism: lincRNA-p21 is itself a direct p53 transcriptional target, and it acts as the effector arm of the p53 repressive program rather than as an activator of Suv39h1. It binds the RNA-binding protein hnRNP-K and delivers it to the promoters of genes that p53 and lincRNA-p21 co-repress — Suv39h1 being one of the validated examples (Huarte et al., Cell 2010). There, hnRNP-K occupancy is required to keep the locus in a repressed state; knock-down of lincRNA-p21 abolishes hnRNP-K binding at the Suv39h1 promoter and releases the gene from repression. So the order is: p53 → induced lincRNA-p21 → hnRNP-K recruitment to the Suv39h1 promoter → transcriptional silencing; remove lincRNA-p21 and the last step fails, giving de-repression. Hence SUV39H1 mRNA rises relative to the matched unperturbed control.

down

SMAD4 is the obligate co-SMAD of the canonical TGF-β/BMP arm: SMAD3 can only carry signal into the nucleus as a SMAD3–SMAD4 heteromer, since SMAD3 lacks a functional nuclear export/import-independent activation mode and the heteromer is what binds SBE (GTCTAGAC-like) elements with high affinity and recruits co-activators (p300/CBP, MED12 in the Mediator complex) to drive transcription. So the order is: TGF-β receptor activation → SMAD3 phosphorylation and nuclear entry → SMAD3–SMAD4 complex formation → SBE occupancy at the PTPRK regulatory region → PTPRK transcription. Removing or reducing SMAD4 does not abolish SMAD3 phosphorylation or nuclear shuttling, but it strips the complex of its transcriptional competence — monomeric SMAD3 has low SBE affinity and cannot efficiently recruit the co-activator machinery. The net effect on the matched unperturbed control is therefore loss of SMAD3-driven transactivation at PTPRK, i.e. decreased PTPRK expression. Note the practical caveat: SMAD4 loss is a strong block on canonical signaling and, if the perturbation is chronic, compensatory non-canonical or SMAD3-independent inputs could partially mask the drop, but the expected acute direction relative to control is down.

down

RELA (p65), the NF-κB activating subunit, binds the intronic NF-κB response element within TBC1D4 and acts as a transcriptional activator, so perturbing that site removes the binding platform and the enhancer cannot deliver its activating signal. Order of events in the unperturbed context: stimulus-driven RELA nuclear translocation → RELA occupancy of the intronic κB site → recruitment of coactivators (p300/CBP, Mediator) and increased RNA Pol II firing at the TBC1D4 promoter → higher TBC1D4 mRNA. With the site disrupted, that step is eliminated while the promoter and other regulatory inputs remain as in the matched control, so TBC1D4 expression falls below control levels — the decrease is enhancer-intrinsic (loss of RELA occupancy), not a secondary effect on NF-κB signaling generally. Expected direction: down.

down

Mechanistically: FOXK1 is a forkhead transcription factor that physically partners with TP63 and co-occupies p63-dependent regulatory elements, where it is required to sustain p63-driven enhancer–promoter looping and transcriptional output. When FOXK1 is removed, the p63–FOXK1 complex at the HNRNPL locus is disrupted, p63 occupancy/activity at that element falls, and TP63-mediated transactivation of HNRNPL is lost — so HNRNPL mRNA declines relative to the matched control. Order of events: FOXK1 loss → loss of the p63–FOXK1 activating complex/chromatin contacts → reduced TP63-dependent transcription at the HNRNPL locus → down.

down

NFE2L2 (Nrf2) is a cap'n'collar bZIP transcription factor that functions as a transcriptional activator: upon stabilization and nuclear import it heterodimerizes with small Maf proteins and binds antioxidant response elements (AREs) in the regulatory regions of its target genes. Txnrd1, encoding thioredoxin reductase 1, is a canonical Nrf2/ARE target that sustains the reduced thioredoxin pool. In a loss- or reduction-of-function setting, the ARE-bound activating complex is depleted, occupancy at the Txnrd1 regulatory element falls, and transcription of the gene drops — the causal order runs NFE2L2 loss → reduced ARE occupancy and transactivation → lower Txnrd1 mRNA → lower TXNRD1 protein and diminished thioredoxin-reducing capacity. The direction is therefore down relative to the matched unperturbed control.

up

The CUL3 intronic element is a ZNF263-bound silencer, and ZNF263 is a KRAB zinc-finger repressor — it does not activate, it recruits the KAP1/TRIM28–HP1 scaffold, which in turn brings in SETDB1 to deposit H3K9me3 and compact the local chromatin. Perturbing that intronic site removes the docking sequence ZNF263 needs, so the causal chain runs: binding site disrupted → ZNF263 occupancy lost → KAP1/HP1/SETDB1 recruitment and H3K9me3 at the locus fall → chromatin decondenses and RNA Pol II access improves → CUL3 transcription rises. Repression was the element's net function, so lifting it releases the gene upward; CUL3 mRNA goes up relative to the matched unperturbed control.

down

miR-10b is a microRNA embedded in the HOXD cluster whose mature guide strand carries a seed match to the 3′ UTR of HOXD10, so loading it into Argonaute/RISC directs post-transcriptional repression of the HOXD10 transcript (mRNA destabilization plus translational block). The causal order in this circuit runs TWIST1 → miR-10b → HOXD10: TWIST1 binds and activates the miR-10b locus, the induced microRNA then acts directly on HOXD10 as its key mediator, and HOXD10 loss in turn feeds back on the TWIST1/miR-10b axis. In the gain-of-function perturbation the microRNA itself is the manipulated node, so the repression step is engaged directly regardless of TWIST1 status: more miR-10b means more RISC loaded onto the HOXD10 3′ UTR and less HOXD10 output relative to the matched unperturbed control. Direction is down whether the readout is transcript or protein, though the protein drop typically exceeds the mRNA drop because microRNAs repress translation as well as promote decay.

up

miR-210 is a hypoxia-inducible microRNA whose transcription is driven directly by HIF1A; among its best-validated targets is the iron–sulfur cluster assembly scaffold ISCU. miR-210 loads into the RISC and pairs with the ISCU 3′UTR, recruiting Argonaute to repress translation and promote transcript destabilization, so under basal conditions ISCU protein and mRNA are held down. When miR-210 is lost or reduced, that repressive RISC complex is no longer recruited to the ISCU 3′UTR, and the de-repressed transcript is translated and accumulates — ISCU rises relative to the matched control. Order of events: HIF1A → miR-210 biogenesis → miR-210-guided RISC binding to ISCU 3′UTR → translational repression/mRNA decay; removing miR-210 reverses the last step, so ISCU expression increases. (Note: HIF1A also directly transactivates ISCU under hypoxia, and this direct arm becomes unmasked once miR-210-mediated repression is lifted, reinforcing the upward direction.)

down

KDM1A (LSD1) is the H3K4me1/2 demethylase that, recruited by hematopoietic repressors (GFI1B and related SNAG-domain factors) and as part of the GATA2/TAL1/LSD1 complex, keeps GATA2 silent in differentiating erythroid cells. Removing KDM1A erases that repression, so its direct target GATA2 is derepressed first; the resulting excess GATA2, acting with TAL1 and residual corepressor machinery at GATA1 regulatory regions, then represses GATA1 transcription. Order of events: KDM1A loss → GATA2 up → GATA1 down, which leaves cells locked in a GATA2-high/GATA1-low progenitor-like state and blocks erythroid maturation.
